title: Spring Boot: app structure, DI, scopes and configuration
description: Spring Boot application structure, auto-configuration, dependency injection and bean scopes, proxy pitfalls, circular references, and typed externalised configuration.
source: Spring Boot reference (auto-configuration, externalised config, circular references in the 2.6 release notes); Spring Framework core documentation (dependencies, @Primary and @Qualifier); Baeldung
seriesTitle: Interview roadmap: Java and Spring Boot
seriesDescription: Java and Spring Boot interview topics in JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short Java/SQL code and multi-correct questions. Java only: nothing here mixes in Python.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which annotations are meta-annotations of @SpringBootApplication?

options.text: @SpringBootConfiguration
options.why: It marks the class as a configuration source, a specialised @Configuration.

options.text: @EnableAutoConfiguration
options.why: It turns on conditional auto-configuration driven by the classpath.

options.text: @ComponentScan
options.why: It scans the annotated class's package and sub-packages for stereotypes.

options.text: @EnableWebMvc
options.why: Not included; adding it would even switch off Boot's MVC defaults.

options.text: @EnableTransactionManagement
options.why: Not included; transaction support comes from auto-configuration instead.

options.text: @EnableAsync
options.why: Not included; @Async needs this annotation added by hand.

questions.explanation: @SpringBootApplication = @SpringBootConfiguration + @EnableAutoConfiguration + @ComponentScan. Because of the component scan, the main class normally sits in the root package; beans in sibling packages above it are not found.

questions.prompt: Judge the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: With spring-boot-starter-data-jpa and the H2 driver on the classpath and no datasource properties, Boot starts with an embedded in-memory DataSource.
questions.reason: Auto-configuration classes are guarded by conditions such as @ConditionalOnClass and @ConditionalOnMissingBean.

whys.a: Correct: the conditions detect H2 on the classpath and the missing DataSource bean, which is why the embedded database appears.
whys.b: Wrong: R is the actual mechanism behind A.
whys.d: Wrong: A is true; embedded DB auto-config is documented behaviour.

questions.explanation: Auto-configuration backs off when you define your own bean (@ConditionalOnMissingBean) and activates on classpath content (@ConditionalOnClass). Use --debug or the conditions report to see what matched.

questions.prompt: A prototype-scoped bean is injected through the constructor into a singleton @Service. After startup the service method that uses it is called 5 times. How many instances of the prototype bean does the container create in total?
questions.explanation: Injection happens once, when the singleton is built, so the singleton keeps that single prototype instance. To get a fresh one per call, inject an ObjectProvider<T>, use a scoped proxy, or a lookup method.

questions.prompt: Fill in the bean scope vocabulary.
questions.text: The default Spring scope is {1}: one shared instance per container. A {2} bean is created anew every time it is requested, and a {3} bean lives for one HTTP request (web applications only).
questions.explanation: Singleton is the default. Prototype beans are not tracked after creation, so their destroy callbacks are not called by the container. Request and session are web scopes.

questions.prompt: Write a Spring service class OrderService, annotated as a service bean, that depends on an OrderRepository through constructor injection (final field, no field injection).
questions.explanation: With a single constructor Spring 4.3+ injects without @Autowired. A final field makes the dependency mandatory and the class easy to unit-test with a plain new. Lombok @RequiredArgsConstructor is an equally valid alternative.

questions.prompt: Judge the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: Calling a @Transactional method from another method of the same class does not start a transaction.
questions.reason: Spring Boot defaults to CGLIB class-based proxies (proxyTargetClass=true).

whys.a: Wrong: CGLIB vs JDK proxy does not explain it; the same bypass happens with both.
whys.b: Correct: both statements are true, but the real cause is that this.method() never goes through the proxy object.
whys.c: Wrong: R is true; Boot has defaulted to CGLIB since 2.0.
whys.d: Wrong: A is true; self-invocation skips the transactional proxy.

questions.explanation: Transactions, @Async, @Cacheable and @Aspect advice are applied by a proxy around the bean. An internal call uses this, not the proxy. Fixes: move the method to another bean, inject the bean's own proxy, or use AspectJ weaving.

questions.prompt: Judge the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: A Spring singleton bean is automatically thread-safe.
questions.reason: Singleton scope means a single shared instance per application context.

whys.a: Wrong: A is false, so R cannot be explaining a true assertion.
whys.c: Wrong: A is false; R is true.
whys.d: Correct: one shared instance is exactly why mutable state in a singleton needs care; Spring adds no synchronisation.

questions.explanation: Singleton means shared, not synchronised. Keep singleton beans stateless or guard their mutable state, a classic interview follow-up.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which statements about Spring Boot externalised configuration are correct?

options.text: A command-line argument --server.port=9000 overrides server.port in application.yml.
options.why: Command-line arguments sit near the top of the property-source order.

options.text: The environment variable SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL binds to spring.datasource.url.
options.why: Relaxed binding maps upper-case underscore names to dotted properties.

options.text: application-prod.yml values override application.yml when the prod profile is active.
options.why: Profile-specific files take precedence over the default file.

options.text: Values in a file packaged inside the jar always beat environment variables.
options.why: Reversed: environment variables override packaged files, which is how containers are configured.

options.text: Setting spring.profiles.active is only possible inside application.yml.
options.why: It can also come from an env var or a command-line flag.

options.text: Profiles can only be used to switch configuration, never beans.
options.why: @Profile on a @Bean or @Component also includes or excludes beans.

questions.explanation: Remember the rule: external wins over packaged, specific wins over general. Keep secrets out of the jar and supply them through env vars or a secrets manager.

questions.prompt: OrderService takes PaymentService through its constructor, and PaymentService takes OrderService through its constructor. What happens when a Spring Boot 3 application starts with default settings?

options.text: Startup fails because the beans are stuck in creation (BeanCurrentlyInCreationException).
options.why: Correct: constructor cycles cannot be resolved, and Boot also prohibits circular references by default.

options.text: Spring injects an early reference through its singleton cache and the application starts normally.
options.why: Early references only helped setter or field injection, and Boot 2.6+ turns even that off by default.

options.text: The application starts, but one of the two fields stays null until first use.
options.why: Spring never leaves a required constructor argument null; it fails fast instead.

options.text: Spring silently switches one of the beans to prototype scope to break the cycle.
options.why: Scopes are never changed automatically; the cycle is simply reported as an error.

questions.explanation: Fix the design (extract a third bean or an event) rather than reaching for spring.main.allow-circular-references=true or @Lazy, which only hide the cycle. Constructor injection is what exposes cycles at startup.

questions.prompt: Two beans of type PaymentGateway exist, and StripeGateway is annotated @Primary. Write the constructor of CheckoutService (one parameter named gw, no Lombok) so that it receives the bean named "paypal" instead of the primary one.

checks.label: uses @Qualifier with the bean name paypal

questions.explanation: An explicit @Qualifier beats @Primary, which only picks a default when nothing narrower is stated. Without either, two candidates throw NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException. Other valid routes: naming the parameter paypal, or injecting List<PaymentGateway> or Map<String, PaymentGateway>.

questions.prompt: Match each Spring Boot construct with its job.

right.text: Registers the bean only when the prod profile is active
Binds a property prefix to a typed object
Runs code once after the context has started
Creates and registers a bean that you build by hand
Schedules a method with a cron expression
Intercepts every HTTP request before the controller

questions.explanation: Profiles switch configuration and beans per environment, ConfigurationProperties gives typed and validated settings, and runners cover startup work.

questions.text: Bind a property prefix to a typed class with {1}; Spring Boot's relaxed binding maps the environment variable {2} onto spring.datasource.url; a single property can be injected with {3}.
questions.explanation: @Value is for single properties and does not support relaxed binding as flexibly. Relaxed binding upper-cases the name and replaces dots and dashes with underscores.

questions.prompt: Write a Spring Boot immutable configuration class MailProps for properties under prefix app.mail with a String host and an int port, as a record bound by @ConfigurationProperties.

checks.label: is a record (or class) named MailProps
has String host and int port

questions.model:
@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "app.mail")
public record MailProps(String host, int port) {}
questions.explanation: Register with @EnableConfigurationProperties(MailProps.class) or @ConfigurationPropertiesScan. Add @Validated and constraints for fail-fast startup.

questions.prompt: A @Service bean with the default scope is injected into three different controllers of one application context. How many instances of that service exist?
questions.explanation: Singleton scope means one shared instance per application context, injected wherever it is requested. Hence the service must be stateless or thread-safe.

questions.prompt: The main class is annotated @SpringBootApplication and lives in package com.acme.app. A @Component class lives in com.acme.shared. With default settings, what happens to it?

options.text: It is registered, because Boot scans every package whose name starts with the same com.acme prefix as the main class.
options.why: Boot scans downwards from the main class package only, not by company prefix.

options.text: It is registered, because @Component classes are discovered through the classpath index.
options.why: Discovery follows the scan base packages, not a global index.

options.text: It is not found by component scanning, because scanning covers only com.acme.app and its sub-packages.
options.why: Correct: the scan starts at the package of the annotated main class.

options.text: Application start fails with a duplicate bean error as the package is outside the root.
options.why: Missing beans cause injection errors later, not a duplicate bean failure at scan time.

questions.explanation: Fix by moving the main class to the root package (com.acme), or by naming extra base packages with scanBasePackages.
